query: Single-phase high-entropy alloys have difficulty achieving a satisfactory strength–ductility balance. Earlier work introduced the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure to enable large-sized production and obtain good strength and plasticity, but its performance still falls short of industrial requirements. Its use in aircraft and spacecraft fasteners further requires stability under extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosion, while relevant creep and corrosion studies remain limited by sample-size and experimental-environment constraints. Given these limitations and design requirements, what single intervention could improve the alloy’s practical performance? Present one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted improvement over the starting material, boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a feasible experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Bulk microalloying of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 with trace amounts (~0.5–1 at%) of reactive elements (specifically Y and Hf) will enhance its high‐temperature stability, room‐temperature creep resistance, and corrosion resistance by promoting the formation of stable nano‐oxide dispersions at phase boundaries without degrading its inherent strength–ductility balance.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high‐entropy alloy with a fine lamellar dual-phase microstructure (fcc/B2 or fcc + L12/B2) that exhibits a commendable strength–ductility synergy but shows limits in creep and corrosion performance under extreme conditions.
generation.intervention: Introduce a small, controlled amount (approximately 0.5–1 atomic percent total) of Y and Hf into the bulk alloy during melting and casting, ensuring uniform distribution so that during subsequent thermo‐mechanical processing these reactive elements segregate to phase boundaries.
generation.conditions: Subject both the microalloyed and baseline alloys to cyclic thermal fluctuations (up to ~700°C), long-term sustained mechanical loading (room-temperature creep tests) and corrosion tests in chloride-containing sulfuric acid solutions (mimicking operational environments such as those in aircraft/spacecraft fasteners).
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of stable, nanometric oxide dispersions (or clusters) at the inherited lamellar (phase boundary) interfaces that serve both to stabilize the microstructure and to retard dislocation motion and boundary migration.
generation.mechanism: The trace reactive elements (Y and Hf) tend to segregate at phase boundaries during solidification and subsequent processing. They form fine oxide clusters that reduce grain boundary diffusion and interfacial mobility. This not only pins the lamellar interfaces (improving creep resistance) but also aids in forming a more robust, stable passive film under corrosive, high-temperature conditions, thereby mitigating pitting and overall degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline EHEA, the microalloyed alloy is expected to show: (1) reduced room‐temperature creep strain rates and extended creep rupture lifetimes under sustained loading; (2) improved corrosion resistance in chloride-containing environments (demonstrated by enhanced passive film stability and reduced pitting at elevated temperatures) while (3) maintaining comparable tensile yield strength and ductility.
generation.baseline: The standard AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high‐entropy alloy produced without Y/Hf microalloying, known to offer a good strength–ductility trade-off yet limited in its long-term mechanical loading (creep) and corrosion performance under extreme temperature variations.
generation.boundary: The improvements are expected if the reactive element content remains within the 0.5–1 at% range and processing conditions (thermal exposures up to ~700°C) do not promote the formation of unwanted coarse intermetallic phases. Deviations in concentration or processing parameters could lead to embrittlement or microstructural coarsening.
generation.uncertainty: This proposal extrapolates benefits observed in coating studies (PMC10488378::web::000::abstract) and discussions on modifying lamellar microstructures (PMC6353877::web::018::discussion) to a bulk alloy system. Uncertainties remain regarding the exact distribution, size, and phase stability of the oxide dispersions in the bulk material under service conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two sets of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloys: one using the standard composition (baseline) and one with an added 0.5–1 at% of Y and Hf, processed under identical thermo‐mechanical routes to develop the lamellar microstructure. Subject both variants to (a) room‐temperature creep tests under sustained loading, (b) cyclic thermal fluctuation tests up to ~700°C combined with mechanical loading, and (c) accelerated corrosion tests in chloride-containing sulfuric acid solutions.
measurements: Morphological and microchemical analysis (TEM/SEM and EDS) to identify the oxide dispersion at phase boundaries
Quantitative creep testing (creep strain vs. time and time-to-rupture)
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy and potentiodynamic polarization measurements to evaluate passive film robustness and pitting tendency
Tensile testing to assess strength–ductility balance
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the microalloyed alloy does not exhibit statistically significant improvements (e.g., >15% slower creep rates and >20% higher polarization resistance or reduced pitting density) compared to the baseline—while maintaining similar tensile strength and ductility—the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

The solidification microstructure, thermal stability, and hot corrosion performance of the coatings at 900 °C under 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl molten salts were investigated. The experimental results showed that the structure of the as-deposited coatings consisted of FCC and BCC/B2 phases. After heat treatment, an Al-rich L12 phase was precipitated in the FCC phase of all coatings. The grain sizes of the EHEA and YHf-EHEA coatings after heat treatment at 900 °C for 10 h increased by 27.5% and 15.7%, respectively, compared to the as-deposited coatings. Meanwhile, after hot corrosion, the spallation areas of the YHf-EHEA and EHEA coatings accounted for 14.98% and 5.67% of the total surface area, respectively. In this work, we successfully achieve a superior strength–ductility combination in AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEAs by introducing two concurrent effects, the two-hierarchical constraint effect and the self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanisms. The underlying origin lying behind the observed mechanical response is the inherited lamellar geometry from the as-cast EHEA. It is known that grain refinement to the nano/ultrafine-grained regime can render material stronger, but this process is usually accompanied by a dramatic loss of ductility. However, with a composite lamellar architecture, the ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure in this study achieves an improved strength–ductility synergy. Phase decomposition is applied to optimize properties instead of just being a phase-instability phenomenon frequently observed in single-phase HEAs, which may encourage further research in this area. In addition, the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA could be simply processed to achieve properties that are an improvement over traditional TRIP (transformation-induced plasticity) and TWIP (twinning-induced plasticity) steels (Fig. 5). Recent studies indicate that eutectic high-entropy alloys can simultaneously possess high strength and high ductility, which have potential industrial applications. The present study focuses on Al0.7CoCrFeNi, a lamellar dual-phase (fcc + B2) precipitation-strengthenable eutectic high entropy alloy. This alloy exhibits an fcc + B2 (B2 with bcc nano-precipitates) microstructure resulting in a combination of the soft and ductile fcc phase together with hard B2 phase. Low temperature annealing leads to the precipitation of ordered L12 intermetallic precipitates within the fcc resulting in enhanced strength. The strengthening contribution due to fine scale L12 is modeled using Orowan dislocation bowing and by-pass mechanism. The alloy was tested under quasi-static (strain-rate = 10−3 s−1) tensile loading and dynamic (strain-rate = 103 s−1) compressive loading. Due to the fine lamellar microstructure with a large number of fcc-bcc interfaces, the alloy show relatively high flow-stresses, ~1400 MPa under quasi-static loading and in excess of 1800 MPa under dynamic loading.
